The README shows several ways to define an enum. Their syntax differs, but the goal stays the same: produce a stable, queryable, UI-friendly enum collection. This page compares them through a single interactive surface.
storybook.stories.CoreInitialization.sec: Different inputs affect the raw source shape, but the core query and transform experience stays consistent.
Pick a value to inspect its label, key, raw payload, and basic summary information.
For UI binding, items are usually the most important runtime shape.
These properties appear repeatedly in later APIs, plugins, and UI bindings.
storybook.stories.CoreInitialization.arr: The README highlights array initialization for API-driven data. This demo maps backend fields into an enum and then back into Select options.
Use getValue / getKey / getLabel to adapt to any backend naming convention.
The same enum can power both business lookup and Ant Design specific field naming.
storybook.stories.CoreApi.metaDescriptio: Focuses on the high-frequency APIs from the README: label, key, raw, findBy, toList, toMap, items, meta, and symbol fallbacks for naming conflicts.
storybook.stories.CoreApi.page.title: Use enums as a real business query layer
storybook.stories.CoreApi.page.descripti: Compared with native enum, enum-plus matters not only at definition time but also because it consolidates querying, display lookup, mapping, and metadata access into one stable object.
storybook.stories.CoreApi.section.overvi: items, values, labels, meta, and named can all feed page rendering or business logic directly.
label, key, raw, has, and findBy are the most common read operations in business code.
storybook.stories.CoreApi.section.transf: toList and toMap are the most common data exits for selects, config maps, and static dictionaries.
Even without a UI plugin, items remain the most stable base data source.
storybook.stories.CoreApi.conflict.metaD: Demonstrates how enum-plus resolves naming collisions when your business fields are named items, keys, values, labels, meta, or named: user data stays intact on the enum object, while the framework capabilities move to exported symbol keys.
When business data collides with built-in enum API names, enum-plus does not force you to rename your fields. It keeps the original fields readable on the enum object and exposes the real enum collections through symbol keys like ITEMS, VALUES, and META.
storybook.stories.CoreApi.conflict.secti: The left side shows business fields that collide with API names. The right side shows the actual enum capabilities on symbol keys.
storybook.stories.CoreCompositionAndExte: Shows how to compose multiple enums into a full workflow with raw(), then attach a shared transform method to every enum instance through Enum.extends.
storybook.stories.CorePatterns.metaDescr: Bundles the more easily overlooked but highly practical README topics together: string localization with autoLabel, and one global template that simplifies labeling for every enum.
storybook.stories.CorePatterns.localizat: This approach also works outside React. With localize, enum labels become resource keys instead of hard-coded display text. A better practice than this example is to install an internationalization plugin library, such as i18next.
Register the global localize function with your custom implementation. Note that this is just an example; in a real project, you should use an internationalization plugin library, such as i18next.
After switching locale, the enum name, select labels, and derived labels update together.
storybook.stories.CoreCompositionAndExte: After merging multiple enums into a full workflow, you can also attach a shared transform method to every enum instance via Enum.extends.
Start with focused enums for each workflow stage, then merge their raw definitions into one larger enum. This keeps the source definitions readable while avoiding duplicated item config.
Use raw() to recover the original definitions, then rebuild a new enum from them.
This demo adds toBadgeMap() through Enum.extends and turns a single enum into status badge ready data.
storybook.stories.CorePatterns.templates: Global templates: one config for every enum
Set Enum.config.templates once, then every enum only needs a minimal init object plus options.name. Keys are derived automatically and localized through Enum.localize.
Locale resources use flat mode, all keys are at the same level
Locale resources use nested mode, keys are organized hierarchically

Through global configuration of templates, the definition of enum internationalization can be greatly simplified, keeping enum definitions minimal. Locale resources exist in both flat and nested modes. Switching the resource mode only changes the template strings and locale resources, while enum definitions remain unchanged.
Three enums initialized with the minimal form. Their names and labels are resolved through the global templates automatically.
With global templates, label keys, prefixes, and enum names no longer need to be written per enum.

storybook.stories.PluginAntd.page.title: Turn enums directly into Ant Design data sources
storybook.stories.PluginAntd.page.descri: The value of @enum-plus/plugin-antd is that you stop rewriting mapping code. Define an enum once and generate Select, Menu, Table filters, and more from the same source.
storybook.stories.PluginAntd.section.bin: A single enum can power multiple controls without writing component-level mapping by hand.
storybook.stories.PluginAntd.field.label: label(value)
storybook.stories.PluginAntd.section.tab: toFilter fits Ant Design Table directly, while toValueMap is useful for Ant Design Pro style valueEnum scenarios.

storybook.stories.PluginReactI18n.metaDe: Based on packages/plugin-react/README, this page uses react-i18next to drive enum labels and combines language switching, Select refresh, and isMatch search into one panel.
storybook.stories.PluginReactI18n.page.d: @enum-plus/plugin-react turns label into React renderable content and listens for react-i18next language changes, so selected values, dropdown options, and enum names refresh automatically. This reactive mechanism is injected at the core, so you don't need any extra setup, such as wrapping the outermost context or manually subscribing to language changes.
storybook.stories.PluginReactI18n.sectio: After switching locale, you do not need to rebuild the component. The selected label and enum name refresh automatically.
When label is no longer a plain string, the plugin matching helpers restore searchability.
storybook.stories.CoreWhyEnumPlus.metaDe: Why enum-plus exists: native TS enum stores a status's value but can't express its label, Select options, filter text, badge color or translations — so that logic gets hand-typed into several independent maps that share no type link and drift apart. This page shows the root cause first, then how one enum source closes the gap.
storybook.stories.CoreWhyEnumPlus.compar: Legacy keeps several parallel maps; enum-plus keeps one definition and derives every output from it.
The same status: scattered maps vs one enum
storybook.stories.CoreWhyEnumPlus.intera: When status rules change, you update one definition instead of synchronizing four or five separate UI maps.
Change one value; every output follows
storybook.stories.CoreWhyEnumPlus.pageDe: It starts with native TypeScript enum: it stores a status's value, but not its user-facing label, its Select options, its filter text, its badge color or its translations. So in every real project that logic is re-typed across labelMap, options, filters and color maps — copies that share no type relation. Change one value and you must hunt down every other copy; miss one and the UI silently lies about the data. This page shows the root cause first, then how enum-plus replaces all of it with one source of truth.
storybook.stories.CoreWhyEnumPlus.pageTi: Why does one status need five hand-written maps?
storybook.stories.CoreWhyEnumPlus.tableD: Both badge text and badge color are derived from the same enum raw/meta data.
storybook.stories.CoreWhyEnumPlus.tableT: The same enum drives actual page rendering

Select needs options, cards need badges, tables need labels plus meta, and config panels need maps. This page shows how one enum can feed all of them at once.

storybook.stories.PluginI18next.metaDesc: Demonstrates the plain i18next integration: enum labels resolve through i18next, while UI refresh still depends on the host framework rerendering.
storybook.stories.PluginI18next.note: This is not a bug. The plugin only connects localize to i18next. Automatic UI refresh should be handled by a React/Vue specific plugin, or listen for language changes in the top-level App component and trigger a full rerender.
storybook.stories.PluginI18next.pageDesc: @enum-plus/plugin-i18next is useful when you want plain enum label localization through i18next. It solves translation lookup, not React/Vue reactivity. To achieve automatic UI refresh, install a React/Vue specific plugin, or listen for language changes in the top-level App component and trigger a full rerender.

storybook.stories.PluginI18next.runtimeD: This demo intentionally changes the i18next language without calling setState. The translation source changes immediately, but the visible UI waits for the next rerender.
storybook.stories.PluginI18next.runtimeT: It solves translation lookup, not refresh propagation. After language changes, the host UI must rerender
storybook.stories.PluginI18next.structur: Even without a UI-specific plugin, the enum can still expose stable outputs like toList, toMap, and raw.
storybook.stories.PluginReactI18next.met: Shows the lightweight react-i18next integration package: it reads translations from the shared React i18n instance, but automatic UI refresh still belongs to plugin-react.

It solves translation lookup, not refresh propagation

storybook.stories.PluginReactI18next.pag: @enum-plus/plugin-react-i18next fits projects that already use react-i18next. It reads translations from the current React i18n instance. To achieve automatic UI refresh, please install the React/Vue specific plugin, or listen for language changes in the top-level App component and trigger a full rerender.
react-i18next: shared React i18n instance, but no automatic UI refresh

storybook.stories.PluginNextInternationa: Shows the client-side next-international integration: PatchedI18nProviderClient wires runtime translation into enum-plus so labels and search can react to locale changes.
The automatic update here comes from the Next International provider, not from rebuilding the enum manually.

@enum-plus/plugin-next-international does more than translate labels. It connects the next-international client runtime to enum-plus, and PatchedI18nProviderClient lets enum text and search follow the active locale.
Next International: connect Next App Router locale context to enum-plus
This page follows the same core idea used in the package tests: build a tiny Next router context, then inject runtime.t into enum-plus through PatchedI18nProviderClient.
isMatch works against the translated text, not the raw locale key.

storybook.stories.PluginVueI18n.derivedD: Even though this story focuses on the localization fallback path, UI-friendly structures like toList, toMap, and items remain reusable.
storybook.stories.PluginVueI18n.note: Inside real Vue components, plugin-vue-i18n can work with useI18n. This story focuses on the smallest framework-independent functional loop.
storybook.stories.PluginVueI18n.pageDesc: plugin-vue-i18n is designed for Vue component environments, but it also exposes an instance fallback. That lets this React-based Storybook still validate the core contract: enum labels resolve through a vue-i18n instance, while visible UI refresh depends on the host rerender.

storybook.stories.PluginI18nextVue.metaD: Shows the i18next-vue integration through its non-component fallback path so the plugin contract can still be demonstrated from Storybook React.

storybook.stories.PluginSample.metaDescr: Explains the plugin authoring model itself by showing how the sample plugin adds one extension method to every enum instance through Enum.extends.
storybook.stories.PluginSample.note: If you later build helpers like toBadgeMap, toStatCard, or business search adapters, they follow the same extension mechanism.
storybook.stories.PluginSample.pageDescr: This plugin is not about business features. It exists to show how plugin authoring works in enum-plus. It uses Enum.extends to add one sample() method to every enum instance, making it the clearest entry point for custom plugin design.

storybook.stories.workbenchDemo.metaDesc: A realistic offline CRUD playground that shows how enum-plus can drive enterprise table filters, modal forms, metadata badges, localized labels, and multiple Ant Design inputs from one enum source of truth.
storybook.stories.workbenchDemo.page.des: The goal is to make enum-plus feel like a real productivity multiplier instead of a toy mapping helper.
storybook.stories.workbenchDemo.page.sho: Scroll to the bottom of the page to see the underlying enum source code.
A support operations desk manages incoming enterprise requests. Product, ops, and success teams need a shared view with consistent labels, filters, status badges, and editing controls.
storybook.stories.workbenchDemo.overview: Everything here is offline and stored in memory, but the interaction model intentionally mirrors a serious internal admin tool: seeded requests, multiple slices, editable forms, and metadata-aware presentation.
The same enums drive Segmented view switching, searchable Select filters, table column filters, and render metadata like badge status and tag color.
raw() and findBy() expose business metadata such as badge color, urgency weight, and field hints, which can be reused by both detail panels and editing experiences.

All UI component data sources on the page are driven by these enums. You don't need to manually transform the data; the enums themselves include methods to automatically generate UI mapping data. This makes enum-plus debuggable while still removing repetitive mapping code.

storybook.stories.CoreWhyEnumPlus.rootTi: The root cause: a vocabulary with no dictionary
storybook.stories.CoreWhyEnumPlus.rootDe: Native TS enum is a value container. The moment you need a user-facing label, a Select option, a filter or a translation, you leave the enum and hand-write another map — each one independent, with no type constraint linking it to the others.
storybook.stories.CoreWhyEnumPlus.rootKp: Places to touch when a value changes
storybook.stories.CoreWhyEnumPlus.rootNo: A single status change means updating several of these by hand. Miss one — no compile error — and the UI quietly disagrees with the data.
